subject: research/society-cheapcue
professional: a senior microeconomic theorist working on costly-signalling games (Spence/Grafen tradition, quantal-response equilibrium, welfare of separating vs pooling equilibria) who also reviews human-robot social-navigation models; first checks: is the differential-cost (single-crossing) condition what separates the types, is the equilibrium unique or start-dependent, is the welfare comparison against the right pooling/no-signal baseline with signal costs counted as deadweight, what term actually drives the welfare loss, and is the result new given the signalling literature

evidence.correctness: The in-model numbers are right. I re-implemented the model from the README and docstrings without importing any repo code (own binomial-memory logit door mean field, own damped signalling fixed point, own cost accounting; scratchpad audit/indep.py) and reproduced every checked figure to 3 dp: yield-all 1.130/1.051/1.000/1.047; table B at rho 1, 0.5, 0.25, 0 (urgent 1.311/0.990/0.837/0.686, normal 1.103, robots 1.335-1.311, crowd 1.201/1.150/1.128/1.107, normal fake 0.025); F (+0.453 / +0.036 / -0.294 / +0.045). The yield-all robot cost 1.000 also follows by hand: robots always yield and w = d = 1, so every robot encounter costs exactly 1. The 2.5% fake rate follows by hand: the normal gain from signalling is r*(gnos-gsig)*k*pN = 0.3*3*pN, and sigmoid(8*(0.142-0.6)) = 0.025. An independent agent-based simulation (own code, 1,000 agents, 1,500 rounds, signals drawn at the equilibrium sU, sN) at rho = 0.25, cN = 0.6 gives urgent 0.831, normal 1.103, robots 1.311 against mean field 0.837/1.103/1.312. Starting the fixed point from 'everyone signals' instead of 'nobody' gives the same equilibrium in all 105 cells (rho x cN x e), and the max fixed-point residual is 1e-10. `experiments/run.py` (66 s) regenerates results.txt byte for byte and figure.py regenerates the SVG byte for byte. Not a 4: the numbers are right for a model whose robot-robot rule drives the welfare headline (see claims, domain).
evidence.completeness: Everything the README lists runs: sections A-G of run.py, the figure, the 6 tests, the README reproduce line (`python3 -m unittest tests/test_model.py` OK). evidence.verification: `cd research/society-cheapcue && /usr/bin/python3.13 -m pytest -q`: 6 passed in 0.88 s. Four mutants via quality_mutate.py: urgent signalling decision uses cN instead of cU, caught; robot-robot cost vs(gQ, gQ) -> vs(gQ, 0), caught; normal people's signal cost charged as cU instead of cN (the 'who pays' line at the heart of the question), SURVIVED; reading error e ignored in the robot-cost block, SURVIVED. No test runs e > 0 although section E and the summary's misreading claim depend on it, and no test pins any number in results.txt beyond sign and ordering checks.
evidence.craft: Read src/society_cheapcue/__init__.py (59 lines), tests/test_model.py, experiments/run.py, figure.py, and the imported society-fakeurgency, society-urgentdoor and society-doorway modules. Small, readable, deterministic. Defects: equilibrium() and summary() are copies of society_fakeurgency.equilibrium/summary with one changed cost line instead of a per-type-cost parameter upstream (copied engine); imports work only by sys.path.insert into sibling research directories (parents[3]), so the pyproject-installed package cannot import; the iteration cap (600) ends silently with no convergence flag (it did converge everywhere I checked); yield_all is expressed as a cost of 9.0 magic number.
evidence.claims: Backed: every number in the README tables and sections B-G (recomputed above), 'rho = 1 reproduces society-fakeurgency' (test and my rerun), 'faking is set by the normal cost alone', deterministic results. Not backed or wrong: (1) README F says robots lose 0.294 because 'they go against non-signallers and collide more', and the headline says the transfer is 'paid by normal people and by the robots themselves'. Decomposed, robots' cost in encounters with people falls from 0.700 to 0.394 under perfect reading; the whole loss is robot-robot meetings, where both robots play gQ = 1 and collide head-on every time (0.3 x 3 = 0.900 vs 0.300 under yield-all). This rule is inherited from society-fakeurgency and not stated anywhere in this README. With robots treating each other as under yield-all (both yield, cost 1), perfect reading moves the crowd by -0.135, not +0.045, and 25 of the 35 cells of table D become favourable to the crowd (range -0.135 to +0.100); G's '+0.850 at 70% robots' becomes -0.130. So 'the crowd ... is worse off than under yield-all in every cell' and 'a reading fleet cannot make this up' are artefacts of an unstated modelling choice. The limitation about weighting robots at zero points at the wrong cause. (2) 'At rho >= 0.75 the cue leaves them no better off' / project.json 'at rho >= 0.75 there is no gain' and lede 'must pay at most about half' hold at cN = 0.6 only: table C gives +0.098 at rho 0.75, cN 0.4 (a fifth of the perfect-reading gain) and section E gives a gain at rho = 1.0 (cN 0.3, +0.018). (3) 'Nothing is reproduced' and no related signalling-welfare work is cited beyond Spence.
evidence.fitness: Could a researcher build on it? The code is small and reproducible, but the result is a re-expression of textbook signalling theory in a toy door game with every key parameter swept (rho, cN) or round (k = 3, d = 1, wu = 3, bs = 8) and no real data. Nearest prior work: Spence (1973) itself shows the separating equilibrium can be Pareto-dominated by pooling; Grafen (1990, J. Theor. Biol. 144:517) gives the differential-cost handicap condition; Bergstrom & Lachmann (1997, Phil. Trans. R. Soc. B 352:609) show costly-signalling equilibria can leave everyone worse off than no signalling; Lachmann, Szamado & Bergstrom (2001, PNAS 98:13189) separate equilibrium cost from differential cost. None is cited, and the finding 'differential cost is needed and separation is a transfer' is what they predict. The one distinctive conclusion (the robots themselves pay, so no cue can make the fleet a win) is the artefact above. A researcher building on it would inherit a wrong conclusion. It is a legacy standalone project (research/_shared/legacy_projects.txt), not part of a programme, far from the PhD+ bar.
evidence.domain: Method matches standard practice in the parts that are textbook: type-specific signal costs give separation exactly as single-crossing predicts (urgent send 0.92 -> 1.00 as rho falls, normal fake fixed at 0.025), signalling costs are counted as deadweight in welfare, quantal (logit) response is a recognised behavioural model, and the equilibrium is unique on the grid (two starts agree). Departures a signalling theorist would flag: robots are modelled as unable to recognise each other and to coordinate at a door (both 'go' with gQ = 1), which dominates the welfare comparison; robot policy is fixed at (gS, gQ) = (0, 1), not optimised (a gQ sweep at rho 0.25, cN 0.6 shows the urgent gain needs gQ >= 0.4 and the crowd cost with robot-robot fixed turns negative from gQ >= 0.6); the logit sharpness bs = 8 means a useless signal is still sent 23% of the time at cost 0.15 (gQ = 0 case), a noise floor that inflates deadweight and is not swept; no equilibrium refinement discussion (Intuitive Criterion) since QRE is used, acceptable but unstated.

defects.what: The welfare headline ('the crowd, robots included, is worse off than under yield-all in every cell', 'paid by normal people and by the robots themselves', 'a reading fleet cannot make this up') is driven by robot-robot meetings in which both robots play gQ = 1 and collide every time (robot-robot cost 3 vs 1 under yield-all), a rule inherited from society-fakeurgency and not stated in this README. Robots' cost with people actually falls (0.700 -> 0.394). With robots treating each other as under yield-all, perfect reading changes the crowd by -0.135 (not +0.045) and 25 of 35 table-D cells favour the crowd. README F attributes the robot loss to collisions with non-signallers.

The rho threshold is stated as general ('at rho >= 0.75 there is no gain', 'must pay at most about half') but holds only at cN = 0.6: table C gives +0.098 at rho 0.75, cN 0.4, and section E a gain at rho 1.0, cN 0.3.

Two seeded mutants survive: charging normal people the urgent cost cU (the 'who pays' line of the question) and dropping the reading error e from the robot-cost block; no test uses e > 0 and none pins a results.txt number.

Prior work on the welfare of separating signalling (Spence 1973's own pooling dominance, Grafen 1990, Bergstrom & Lachmann 1997, Lachmann, Szamado & Bergstrom 2001) is not cited; the separation-as-transfer finding is what that literature predicts, and novelty is not stated.

Robot policy is fixed at (gS, gQ) = (0, 1) and logit sharpness bs = 8 is not swept; at gQ = 0 a useless cue is still sent 23% of the time at cost 0.15, a noise floor that adds deadweight to every reader cell.
rho, cN and the door costs (k = 3, d = 1, wu = 3) are swept or round figures with no source; disclosed in Limitations.

equilibrium() and summary() are copies of society_fakeurgency's with one changed cost line; imports resolve only via sys.path.insert into sibling research dirs, so the declared package cannot import when installed; the 600-iteration cap ends silently.

verdict: The numbers reproduce exactly: an independent re-implementation, an independent agent-based simulation and a two-start uniqueness check all agree with results.txt, which regenerates byte for byte. Two of four seeded mutants survive, including charging normal people the urgent cost. It misses the bar on what the numbers are said to mean. The headline that the crowd, robots included, is worse off than under yield-all in every cell, and that the robots themselves pay, comes from robot-robot meetings in which both robots always go and collide (cost 3 against 1 under yield-all), a rule this README never states. Robots actually do better with people under the reader policy (0.700 to 0.394). If robots treat each other as they do under yield-all, perfect reading helps the crowd (-0.135, not +0.045) and 25 of the 35 cells turn favourable. The 'rho at most about half' threshold holds at cN = 0.6 only, and the separation-as-transfer result is standard signalling theory (Spence 1973, Bergstrom and Lachmann 1997), none of it cited beyond Spence. The model is sound and reproducible, but its one distinctive conclusion is an artefact.
